subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?
items.correct: The products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants
items.misconception: The reaction goes fully forwards and then it goes fully backwards
items.why: Everyday reversible things are sequential - a swing goes out then comes back, a video plays then rewinds - so students import that one-after-the-other picture into chemistry. The specification says the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. That is possible from the moment any product exists, so the two directions overlap in time.
items.random_wrong: The reaction finishes with equal amounts of reactants and products

items.q: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does the ⇌ symbol tell you?
items.correct: That the reaction can go in the forward and the reverse direction
items.misconception: That the mixture holds equal amounts of A, B, C and D throughout it
items.why: The arrow looks symmetrical and is often drawn with two arrows of equal length, which invites students to read symmetry in the picture as symmetry in the amounts. The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction, so they are usually not equal at all.
items.random_wrong: That the mixture has already reached equilibrium at every moment

items.q: A sample of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white. What must be done to turn it blue again?
items.correct: Add water to the white solid, changing the conditions back again
items.misconception: Nothing will work, as the direction is fixed once heating has started
items.why: Most reactions students meet before this topic run to completion in one direction, so they treat direction as a permanent property of the reaction rather than something set by the conditions. The specification states that the direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions, as when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and then has water added again.
items.random_wrong: Heat the white solid much more strongly for a longer period of time

items.q: Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride is given as an example of a reversible reaction. White ammonium chloride is heated in a tube and the two gases form. Which statement about this example is correct?
items.correct: Cooling the gases re-forms ammonium chloride
items.misconception: The ammonium chloride has been destroyed for good
items.why: Most reactions students meet before this topic run to completion in one direction, so they treat direction as a permanent property of the reaction rather than something set by the conditions. The specification states that the direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions, as when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and then has water added again.
items.random_wrong: Half of the solid always stays behind unchanged

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What can be said about the reverse reaction?
items.correct: It is endothermic and transfers the same amount of energy as the forward one
items.misconception: It is exothermic as well and transfers the same amount of energy back
items.why: Students learn to label a reaction exothermic or endothermic as if it were a fixed property of the substances, so they attach the label to the reaction rather than to a direction. Reversing the change reverses the energy transfer: what was given out on the way forwards must be taken in on the way back.
items.random_wrong: It is endothermic but it transfers less energy than the forward one

items.q: Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate to form white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water takes in 45 kJ of energy. Water is then added to the white solid. What happens to the energy?
items.correct: 45 kJ is given out, as the same amount of energy is transferred
items.misconception: Less than 45 kJ is given out, because some energy is lost as heat
items.why: Students transfer everyday experience of wasted energy in machines, and half-remembered ideas about efficiency, to a chemical change where the specification states the amounts are equal. The specification says the same amount of energy is transferred in each case, so the reverse reaction releases exactly what the forward reaction took in.
items.random_wrong: 45 kJ is taken in, because this change also needs energy

items.q: A reversible reaction takes place in a sealed flask. When is the mixture at equilibrium?
items.correct: When the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
items.misconception: When both the forward and the reverse reactions have completely stopped
items.why: Nothing appears to change once equilibrium is reached, and students take an unchanging observation to mean that nothing at all is happening. Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate; a rate of zero is not what the specification describes.
items.random_wrong: When the amounts of all the reactants and of all the products are the same

items.q: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus that prevents reactants and products escaping if equilibrium is to be reached?
items.correct: Escaped products cannot take part in reverse reactions
items.misconception: The forward reaction stops as soon as any gas is able to leave
items.why: Students focus on the two reactions and overlook the apparatus, so the condition about preventing escape is treated as a detail rather than as part of the definition. If a product escapes it cannot take part in the reverse reaction, so the reverse rate can never rise to match the forward rate and equilibrium is never reached.
items.random_wrong: Equilibrium means nothing at all is allowed to move about

items.q: The same reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium at two different temperatures. What can be said about the amounts of the substances present?
items.correct: The relative amounts of the reactants and products depend on the conditions
items.misconception: The amounts must be equal at equilibrium whatever conditions are used
items.why: The word equilibrium is used in everyday speech and in physics for balanced forces of equal size, so students expect equal quantities rather than equal rates. What is equal at equilibrium is the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction, not the amounts of the substances.
items.random_wrong: The amounts depend only on how quickly equilibrium was reached

items.q: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. According to the specification, how does the system respond?
items.correct: It responds in the direction that counteracts the change that was made
items.misconception: It responds until the change made to it has been cancelled out completely
items.why: The word counteract is read as cancel, and students who have met feedback in other subjects expect a system to restore its starting point exactly. The system responds to counteract the change, which shifts the position of equilibrium and gives new amounts of the substances rather than the original ones.
items.random_wrong: It stays exactly as it was, because it is already at equilibrium

items.q: What can Le Chatelier's Principle be used for?
items.correct: Predicting the effect of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium
items.misconception: Calculating the exact amount of each product present at the new equilibrium
items.why: Students want a rule that produces a number, and the principle is introduced next to calculations on yield, so they expect it to be quantitative. The specification asks only for qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when appropriate information is given.
items.random_wrong: Predicting how long a given mixture will take to reach equilibrium again

items.q: In a sealed flask N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. More nitrogen is pumped into the flask at constant temperature. What is the qualitative prediction?
items.correct: More ammonia forms at the new equilibrium
items.misconception: Less ammonia is present at the new equilibrium
items.why: Students picture the equilibrium as tipping towards whichever side is made heavier, treating it as a balance of amounts rather than as a system that opposes the change. The system counteracts the increase by using up some of the added reactant, and using it up means forming more product.
items.random_wrong: The amount of ammonia present cannot change

items.q: The concentration of one substance in a mixture at equilibrium is changed. What happens to the concentrations of the other substances?
items.correct: They all change until equilibrium is reached again in the mixture
items.misconception: Only the substance whose concentration was altered is different
items.why: Students treat the substances as separate stores rather than as a linked system, so a change to one is not expected to reach the others. Once the system is no longer at equilibrium both reactions run at different rates, and that changes the concentrations of every substance in the mixture.
items.random_wrong: They stay the same, as the system is always at equilibrium

items.q: For the equilibrium CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, more ethanol (C2H5OH) is added. What happens?
items.correct: More products form until equilibrium is reached again in the flask
items.misconception: More reactants form, because ethanol was added to the reactant side
items.why: Students picture the equilibrium as tipping towards whichever side is made heavier, treating it as a balance of amounts rather than as a system that opposes the change. The system counteracts the increase by using up some of the added reactant, and using it up means forming more product.
items.random_wrong: Nothing changes at all, since the total mass has not altered

items.q: In the equilibrium 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, sulfur trioxide (SO3) is continuously removed from the mixture. What happens?
items.correct: More reactants react until equilibrium is reached again
items.misconception: More reactants form, because there is now less product present
items.why: The same tipping-balance picture is used: less on the product side is read as the balance falling towards the reactant side. The system counteracts the loss by replacing some of the product, which means more reactants react and the position of equilibrium moves towards the products.
items.random_wrong: Nothing happens, because the system stays at equilibrium

items.q: A sealed flask holds an equilibrium mixture of hydrogen, iodine and hydrogen iodide: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI. Extra hydrogen is injected and the flask is left until equilibrium is reached again. What is found?
items.correct: More HI, and less iodine than there was
items.misconception: Less HI, and more iodine than there was before
items.why: Students picture the equilibrium as tipping towards whichever side is made heavier, treating it as a balance of amounts rather than as a system that opposes the change. The system counteracts the increase by using up some of the added reactant, and using it up means forming more product.
items.random_wrong: The same HI and the same iodine as before

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?
items.correct: It increases, because the reaction is endothermic in the forward direction
items.misconception: It decreases, because raising the temperature will release more energy
items.why: Students remember that the system counteracts the change but then choose the direction that releases more energy into an already hotter system, reversing the logic. Adding energy is counteracted by taking energy in, so the endothermic direction is favoured; for an exothermic forward reaction that is the reverse direction.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, because the reactants are used up much more quickly

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?
items.correct: It decreases, because the forward reaction gives out energy
items.misconception: It increases, because the forward reaction is the exothermic one
items.why: Students remember that the system counteracts the change but then choose the direction that releases more energy into an already hotter system, reversing the logic. Adding energy is counteracted by taking energy in, so the endothermic direction is favoured; for an exothermic forward reaction that is the reverse direction.
items.random_wrong: It increases, since heating always improves any yield

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?
items.correct: It decreases, as the endothermic direction is no longer favoured
items.misconception: It increases, as cooling a mixture always drives the reaction onwards
items.why: Cooling is associated with reactions slowing down and stopping, so students expect less of everything rather than a shift in position. The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases on cooling for an exothermic reaction, which is why some industrial equilibria are run cool.
items.random_wrong: It increases, as the system must give out energy when it cools down

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?
items.correct: It increases, as the forward reaction is exothermic
items.misconception: It decreases, as a cooler mixture must form less product
items.why: Cooling is associated with reactions slowing down and stopping, so students expect less of everything rather than a shift in position. The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases on cooling for an exothermic reaction, which is why some industrial equilibria are run cool.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, as the endothermic direction is favoured

items.q: For 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. A sealed tube of the mixture is placed in iced water and the brown colour of NO2 fades. What does this show?
items.correct: Cooling has increased the relative amount of the product N2O4
items.misconception: Cooling has stopped both of the reactions in the sealed tube
items.why: Nothing appears to change once equilibrium is reached, and students take an unchanging observation to mean that nothing at all is happening. Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate; a rate of zero is not what the specification describes.
items.random_wrong: Cooling has moved the equilibrium towards the reactant NO2

items.q: For the gaseous equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
items.correct: Towards the ammonia, the side with the fewer molecules
items.misconception: Towards nitrogen and hydrogen, the side with more molecules
items.why: Students link high pressure with more gas being pushed into the vessel, and choose the side with more molecules without asking what would counteract the change. Fewer gas molecules exert less pressure, so shifting to the side with the smaller number of molecules is what counteracts an increase in pressure.
items.random_wrong: Neither way, as pressure cannot alter this mixture

items.q: For the gaseous equilibrium 2SO3(g) ⇌ 2SO2(g) + O2(g), the pressure is decreased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
items.correct: To the right, the side with three molecules of gas
items.misconception: To the left, towards the side with just two gas molecules
items.why: Students link high pressure with more gas being pushed into the vessel, and choose the side with more molecules without asking what would counteract the change. Fewer gas molecules exert less pressure, so shifting to the side with the smaller number of molecules is what counteracts an increase in pressure.
items.random_wrong: Neither way, since the numbers of atoms are equal here

items.q: A student is given the equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), all gases, and increases the pressure on the sealed vessel. What should the student predict?
items.correct: No shift, as each side has two molecules
items.misconception: A shift to the right, towards the hydrogen iodide
items.why: Students link high pressure with more gas being pushed into the vessel, and choose the side with more molecules without asking what would counteract the change. Fewer gas molecules exert less pressure, so shifting to the side with the smaller number of molecules is what counteracts an increase in pressure.
items.random_wrong: A shift to the left, towards hydrogen and iodine

items.q: Does reaching equilibrium mean all of the reactants have been used up?
items.correct: No. Reactants and products are all present at equilibrium; their relative amounts depend on the conditions.
items.misconception: At equilibrium the reaction has finished, so only products are left in the container.
items.why: Students equate the end of any observable change with the end of the reaction, which for one-way reactions usually does mean the reactants are gone. Both reactions are still occurring at equilibrium, which is only possible if reactants and products are both present in the mixture.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does raising the temperature always increase the amount of product at equilibrium?
items.correct: No. It increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction but decreases it for an exothermic reaction.
items.misconception: Heating a reaction always gives more product, because heating makes reactions go better.
items.why: In rates work, raising the temperature always speeds a reaction up, and students carry that always-more result across to the amounts present at equilibrium. Temperature changes the position of equilibrium in a direction that depends on which way the reaction is exothermic, so the effect on the yield can go either way.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, how do you decide which side has fewer molecules?
items.correct: Add the balancing numbers on each side: three molecules on the left and two on the right.
items.misconception: Compare the masses or the numbers of atoms rather than the numbers of molecules.
items.why: Atom counting is drilled hard when balancing equations, so students reach for atoms, and mass is what they are used to conserving. The specification says the number of molecules is shown by the symbol equation, which means the balancing numbers in front of each formula.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What happens to the position of equilibrium when the pressure is increased?
items.correct: Nothing. There are two gas molecules on each side, so neither side is favoured.
items.misconception: The equilibrium shifts, because a pressure change always moves the position of equilibrium.
items.why: The rule is remembered as pressure always has an effect, and students apply it without checking the numbers of molecules in the symbol equation. A pressure change shifts the position of equilibrium only where the two sides have different numbers of gas molecules.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A change is made to a system at equilibrium. Is a shift in position the same as a change in rate?
items.correct: No. A shift changes the relative amounts present at equilibrium, which is not the same as how fast equilibrium is reached.
items.misconception: Any change that speeds a reaction up must also give more product at equilibrium.
items.why: Rates and equilibrium are taught side by side and both use the same conditions, so students merge going faster with going further. The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions, and a condition can change the rate without favouring either direction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.6.2 Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
